title: Overconfident by design
author: David Didau
source: David Didau: The Learning Spy (daviddidau.substack.com), February 11, 2026
summary: David Didau argues that overconfidence is not simply a character flaw but a predictable by-product of missing knowledge and poor feedback conditions. He opens with historical disasters -- the Titanic's missing lifeboats, the Bay of Pigs invasion, and the Challenger shuttle explosion -- to show how confident judgment can outrun the evidence behind it, then notes that roughly ninety percent of people rate themselves better than an average driver, revealing how pervasive the pattern is. Drawing on Dunning and Kruger's research, he explains that the least skilled are often the most certain because the same lack of knowledge that produces errors also prevents people from recognizing them, while the most skilled tend to underestimate their own relative standing. Didau extends this into Robin Hogarth's distinction between "kind" learning environments, where feedback is fast and clear and confidence gets calibrated by reality, and "wicked" environments, where feedback is delayed, noisy or absent and confidence grows untethered from accuracy. Even experts are not immune: he cites research on radiologists whose confidence rose with experience without a matching rise in diagnostic accuracy. The free portion of the piece closes by setting up a broader argument that overconfidence, rather than being purely destructive, may also function as a kind of fuel that gets people to act under uncertainty; the remainder is behind a paywall.
points: Overconfidence is reframed as a predictable symptom of missing knowledge and poor feedback conditions, not a fixed character trait -- a claim with direct implications for how teachers read student certainty.

Dunning and Kruger's refined finding is that poor performers lack the very knowledge needed to judge their own performance, which is why the least skilled are often the most certain and improve their self-insight only as their skill improves.

Hogarth's kind-versus-wicked learning environments framework explains why confidence tracks accuracy in domains with fast, clear feedback (chess, meteorology) but drifts away from accuracy in domains with delayed or ambiguous feedback (politics, investing, management).

Even domain experts aren't protected: radiologists' confidence in diagnoses rose with experience without a corresponding rise in accuracy, showing that fluency and correctness can diverge even among specialists.
The near-universal "I'm better than average" bias (roughly 90% of drivers) demonstrates that self-judgment is a poor proxy for genuine competence whenever objective feedback is absent.
quotes: Overconfidence has an impressive roll call of victims. Notoriously, the builders of the Titanic were so certain of their ship's invincibility that lifeboats were an afterthought. We all know how that ended.
It is well established that around ninety percent of people believe they are better than the average driver. The same logically impossible pattern turns up wherever self judgement is invited.

In their original studies, people who performed worst on tests of grammar, logical reasoning, and humour were also the most likely to rate their performance as above average. Those in the bottom quartile not only made the most mistakes, they appeared largely unaware that they were doing so.

Poor performers were not especially vain or foolish, rather, they lacked knowledge about the standards by which performance should be judged. Crucially, when their skill improved, self insight improved with it.

Studies of medical expertise show that experienced radiologists often become faster and more confident in their judgements without becoming more accurate at detecting subtle cancers. Experience improves fluency and decisiveness, but accuracy can plateau while confidence continues to rise.
In kind domains, feedback is frequent, timely, and unambiguous. Actions lead to clear outcomes and errors are hard to ignore.
Wicked domains are different. Feedback is delayed, noisy, or incomplete. Outcomes depend on many interacting factors and it is rarely obvious which judgement caused which result.
The feeling of certainty reflects how fluent the judgement feels, not how accurate it is.
